feedback: If a learner names £10 as the price: draw the percentage bar and shade discount vs part-left — 'you found the bit taken OFF; the price is the bit that STAYS'. Ask 'what does the shopper actually hand over?'

If a learner leaves 0.75 or 75 as the answer: ask '0.75 of WHAT?' and require conversion to £30 stated as money — a percentage answer ends in the unit of the quantity it is a percentage of, which here is pounds

If a learner subtracts 25 ('25% off means take 25') to get £15: anchor the percentage to the bar of £40 — 25% is a quarter OF this strip = £10 — and contrast 25% of £40 (=£10) with 25% of £80 (=£20) to show it depends on the amount

If a learner reports the carpet answer in a length unit (cm or m) or adds the sides for an area question: keep area and length physically distinct — coverage of the floor is a squared unit (m² or cm²), the edge measured is a length (m or cm) — and do not proceed until the unit matches the quantity, with the squared area unit matching the length unit used (a room measured in metres gives m², so 4 m × 3 m = 12 m²)
activities.intendedInsight: When the question asks what the shopper pays, the answer is the part that STAYS (£30), not the part taken off (£10) nor the bare proportion (0.75); and a model is chosen to fit a situation's structure, with every answer returned to its real units and sense-checked.
learnerActions: Take a situation such as 'a £40 jacket has 25% off — what does a shopper pay?' and first choose which representation exposes its structure from a palette: percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line, or ratio table
Build a percentage bar: partition the 100% strip into quarters, shade off one quarter (the discount), and read what remains
State explicitly what each number refers to: £10 is the discount (25% of £40), 0.75 is the proportion of the original price remaining, and £30 is the price paid
Pass an interpret-back gate: state the final answer with its unit (£30) and check it is reasonable — a sale price must be less than £40

Re-run the same process on a room-carpet problem (choose a scale diagram, apply the area formula, and give the area in a squared unit that matches the length unit of the measurements — e.g. a 4 m × 3 m room needs 12 m² of carpet) and a recipe-scaling problem (choose a double number line, answer in grams)
Notice which representation you reach for — if you grab a single bar for a rate problem that has two varying quantities, ask whether it hides structure
activities.title: Choose, build, interpret back: a modelling workbench

feedback: Reject a bare '10' or '0.75' and ask the learner to say what each number refers to before accepting any answer
If the learner cannot justify plausibility, prompt: 'is the price you pay bigger or smaller than £40, and why must that always be true for a sale?'
activities.intendedInsight: The reflective close of the modelling cycle can be spoken: you name which number is the discount, which is the proportion, and which is the quantity asked for, and you justify that it is sensible.
learnerActions: Work in role with a customer or decorator who only accepts an answer once it is stated as the real quantity they need
Answer the shopkeeper's probe 'you said 30 — is that the discount or what I pay?' by distinguishing the two
Answer the decorator's probe 'is that enough for a 4 m by 3 m room?' by stating an area with its unit (12 m²) and checking it is plausible
Voice the reasonableness check aloud: '£30 — less than £40, so for a sale it makes sense'
activities.title: Defend the answer to a customer or tradesperson

feedback: If a learner gives a length where an area is needed, or drops the squared unit, return to the physical distinction: coverage fills the floor (a squared unit), the edge runs around it (a length unit), and the squared unit must match the length unit used
activities.intendedInsight: Area (coverage) and perimeter (edge length) are physically different quantities with different units; blurring them is the error, not a detail.
learnerActions: Cover the floor of a room to feel area as coverage, reported in a squared unit matching the measurements (e.g. m² of carpet needed for a metre-dimensioned room)
Measure around the edge of the same floor to feel length, reported as a length matching the measurements (e.g. m of skirting or edging)
Say out loud which quantity a given question asks for before computing, and match the unit to it
activities.title: Feel area as coverage, length as edge (optional spatial scaffold)
